correctness.rationale: For a deterministic date s, solve P'=q−(q+μ)P with P(0)=0, then set q=ae^(rs), t=H−s and y=q+μ. This gives F(s)=q(1−exp(−yt))/y. Differentiating with q'=rq and t'=−1 gives F'=q exp(−yt)(rB−1). To check the critical strict inequality independently, put x=yt, p=μ/y and z=exp(x)−1. Then yB=(1−p)x+pz, B_t=1+pz, and yqB_q=p(1−p)[(x−2)z+2x]. Expanding gives y(B_t B−qB_q)=p²z(z+1)+p(1−p)(3z−x)+(1−p)²x>0 for t>0. Thus at any zero of G(s)=rB−1 before H, its derivative is strictly negative, using r=1/B at the zero. With G(H)=−1, two downward zeros would force an intervening non-downward zero, which is impossible. At r=r_c the endpoint zero itself has negative derivative. This proves uniqueness in both regimes including r=0, without assuming that G is globally decreasing. The identity B=t+μ∫₀ᵗ(t−u)exp((q+μ)u)du proves strict decrease of r_c in a,μ,H and r_c<1/H. The no-extinction expression reduces to maximizing ae^(rs)(H−s) and gives the stated comparison. Independent bisection for a=μ=H=r=1 gave s*=0.364045975707 and occupancy 0.464936881234 versus 0.432332358382 at zero, with r_c=0.476811688088. At r=0.6 with those other parameters, delay still wins, directly illustrating the sub-unit rH regime. value.rationale: With a fixed census, interest improves later colonization while waiting removes occupancy time, and even this one-target tradeoff is not decided by a general first-order condition alone. The exact unique-optimum classification isolates the effect of extinction: increasing it strictly lowers the rate required to justify waiting, even below the no-extinction rH=1 threshold. It provides a motivated analytic benchmark separating colonization and extinction effects, without implying that delay improves spatial conservation outcomes generally.
